rationales.are: You takes are for one addressee as well as for several addressees.

rationales.have: We takes have, whether it refers to two people or a larger group.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes do-negation from be-negation with a plural pronoun.

items.setupText: Two British English drafts describe visitors at an entrance: 'The group was waiting' and 'The group were waiting.'

Both are standard, with a unit or a member-focused reading.
Was is correct only if exactly one visitor is waiting.
Were is a past-tense error because group has no written plural ending.
items.answer: Both are standard, with a unit or a member-focused reading.
items.explanation: British English permits singular or plural agreement with many collective nouns, depending on how the group is viewed.

rationales.Were necessarily changes the meaning fro: Plural agreement can reflect the members of one collective; it need not introduce several groups.
rationales.Both are standard, with a unit or a memb: British English permits singular or plural agreement with many collective nouns, depending on how the group is viewed.
rationales.Was is correct only if exactly one visit: A single group can contain many people and still take singular agreement.

items.setupText: A colleague says, 'Neither of the answers explain the procedure.' You are adapting the comment for a conventionally formal report.
items.taskText: Which editorial response is best?

Keep explain because the nearer answers is the main subject of the sentence.
Replace neither with both while keeping the intended negative claim about the answers.
Use does not explain because neither needs a negative auxiliary to convey the intended meaning.
items.answer: Use formal explains here; the spoken plural is also established usage.

rationales.Use formal explains here; the spoken plu: Formal editing normally favors singular agreement with neither of; plural agreement is nevertheless common in less formal usage.

items.setupText: A software help page says, 'Your data is stored locally.' No publisher rule requires plural treatment of data.

Data can take singular agreement when treated as uncountable information.
Are would necessarily change the subject from information to several databases.

rationales.Data can take singular agreement when tr: Data has both plural and mass-singular uses; absent a contrary house rule, this software sentence need not be corrected.

items.setupText: An editor writes, 'More than one visitor has asked about the missing display.'

Has agrees with the singular missing display at the end of the sentence.
Has is permitted only because visitor refers to an unidentified person.

The singular version is possible only if one design was submitted.

items.setupText: A journal consistently treats data as plural. A new sentence begins 'A complete set of these data ...'.

The main subject is singular because set is its head, even under the journal's plural-data rule.
The main subject is singular only if the set contains one datum.
items.answer: The main subject is singular because set is its head, even under the journal's plural-data rule.

rationales.The main subject is singular because set: A complete set is the head phrase; plural these data belongs inside its of complement and does not determine the main verb.
rationales.The main subject must be plural because: That policy governs data when it controls agreement, not every larger phrase containing the word.

items.setupText: A budget report describes the use of funding and the participation of named staff members.
items.taskText: Choose the standard written pair: Sixty percent of the funding ___ allocated, and sixty percent of the staff members ___ enrolled.
items.explanation: Percentage subjects take agreement suited to what is measured: funding is singular mass, staff members plural count.

rationales.is / are: Percentage subjects take agreement suited to what is measured: funding is singular mass, staff members plural count.

items.setupText: An article uses the phrase the unemployed to refer to people without jobs.
items.taskText: Which explanation supports 'The unemployed are eligible for the scheme'?
options: Are is required because eligible is a plural adjective.
The article the makes every following subject plural.
The adjective phrase names a group of people and takes plural agreement.
Are makes the phrase refer to several unemployment programmes.
items.answer: The adjective phrase names a group of people and takes plural agreement.
items.explanation: The unemployed is a conventional adjective-based expression for people as a class, so the verb is plural.

rationales.Are is required because eligible is a pl: English adjectives such as eligible do not take plural endings or control the subject's number.
rationales.The article the makes every following su: The occurs with singular and plural subjects; it does not determine number by itself.
rationales.The adjective phrase names a group of pe: The unemployed is a conventional adjective-based expression for people as a class, so the verb is plural.
rationales.Are makes the phrase refer to several un: The subject denotes people, not the schemes for which they may qualify.

findings: The list of lesson plans merely substituted a noun and repeated crude auxiliary errors.
audit.microSkill: An adjective-based human class subject
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes a plural subject without an overt plural noun.
audit.levelReason: The learner must interpret a nominalized adjective rather than match an -s suffix.

items.setupText: A formal memoir says, 'Many a visitor has paused at that window.'
items.taskText: Which account preserves both the grammar and the meaning?

The sentence refers to one unusually frequent visitor.
Has shows that many a must be changed to a single.
Many a is a plural noun phrase that requires have in a memoir.
items.answer: The expression refers to many visitors but uses singular noun and verb forms.
items.explanation: Many a is a formal distributive expression: the quantity is large, but each imagined visitor is grammatically singular.

rationales.The sentence refers to one unusually fre: Many a distributes the experience over many visitors; it does not describe repeated visits by one person.
rationales.Has shows that many a must be changed to: Singular agreement is normal in many a plus a singular noun and does not require reducing the number meant.
rationales.Many a is a plural noun phrase that requ: The formal construction conventionally uses a singular noun and singular agreement.
rationales.The expression refers to many visitors b: Many a is a formal distributive expression: the quantity is large, but each imagined visitor is grammatically singular.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains the deliberate singular forms without mistaking them for a one-person meaning.
audit.levelReason: A literary-formal quantifier requires interpretation beyond everyday many visitors.
audit.similarityNote: Many a in a memoir, distinct from the numeric more than one construction.

items.setupText: A house style uses agreement with the nearer alternative in either/or subjects of mixed number.

Either the assistants or the director are attending.
Either the director or the assistants is attending.
Either the assistants or the director have confirmed.

rationales.Either the assistants or the director ar: With the singular director nearest, that convention calls for is.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Applies a declared mixed-number rule without pretending all usage conventions are identical.
audit.levelReason: The number and order of two alternative subjects must be tracked.
audit.similarityNote: Mixed-number disjunction, extending B1's two singular either/or subjects.

items.setupText: A report mentions the directors-general of two separate agencies.
items.taskText: Which explanation supports 'The directors-general have approved the exchange'?
options: General refers to all the directors together, so it makes the subject singular.
Have agrees with the plural agencies mentioned in the context rather than the subject.
Directors is the plural head of the compound subject.
The hyphen makes have possible even if there is just one director-general.
items.answer: Directors is the plural head of the compound subject.
items.explanation: The compound title pluralizes director, so directors-general denotes multiple office-holders and takes have.

rationales.General refers to all the directors toge: General is part of the title and does not override the plural head directors.
rationales.Have agrees with the plural agencies men: The actual subject directors-general already supplies plural number; agreement does not depend on an earlier contextual noun.
rationales.Directors is the plural head of the comp: The compound title pluralizes director, so directors-general denotes multiple office-holders and takes have.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Finds the number-bearing noun inside a multiword title.

items.setupText: A tutor contrasts 'Planning and testing are separate stages' with 'Planning and testing is one integrated process in our workshop.'
items.taskText: Which comment best explains the agreement contrast?

The plural version refers to many workshops, and the singular to one.
Plural treats them as separate activities; singular presents their combination as one process.
The first sentence changes the activities into finished past events.
items.answer: Plural treats them as separate activities; singular presents their combination as one process.
items.explanation: Coordinated activities normally take plural agreement, but a clearly unified activity can receive singular notional agreement.

rationales.The singular version is possible only be: Workshop is inside a later prepositional phrase and does not control the subject's agreement.
rationales.The plural version refers to many worksh: The number contrast concerns the activities or their combination, not the number of workshops.

rationales.Plural treats them as separate activitie: Coordinated activities normally take plural agreement, but a clearly unified activity can receive singular notional agreement.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Allows meaning-based singular agreement rather than applying and always plural mechanically.
audit.levelReason: Two complete readings show how conceptual grouping can affect agreement.

items.setupText: An editor is discussing the exact wording 'The offices are closed', not the events the sentence reports.

'The offices is closed' is printed at the top of the notice.
'The offices are closed' is printed at the top of the notice.
'The offices is closed' are printed at the top of the notice.
items.answer: 'The offices are closed' is printed at the top of the notice.

rationales.'The offices are closed' is printed at t: The quotation is one piece of wording, so the outside verb is singular is. The original are remains inside the preserved quotation.
rationales.'The offices are closed' are printed at: This preserves the words but incorrectly lets plural offices control the outside verb, whose subject is the single quotation.

rationales.'The offices is closed' are printed at t: This changes the required quotation and uses plural outside agreement for one quoted sentence. Both conflict with the editing task.

findings: The list-of-agendas item was another simple attraction frame with the same malformed foils.
audit.microSkill: Internal agreement versus agreement when a whole sentence is quoted as an object of discussion
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates the grammatical number inside a quotation from the number of quotations mentioned.
audit.levelReason: The sentence contains two agreement domains that must not be confused.

items.setupText: The delayed issue is whether two venues can open, rather than the venues themselves.

rationales.is: The whether clause names one unresolved issue and takes singular main-clause agreement.
rationales.have been: Have would give plural agreement to the single clausal subject; has been would be grammatical with a different tense.

findings: The group-visitors sentence repeated a variety-sensitive false rejection with a quarterly-summary tail.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids an absolute is-only or are-only rule for a recognized variable construction.

items.setupText: One figure in the budget covers both repair work and inspection work. The report says, 'The cost of repairs and inspections has risen.'
items.taskText: Which analysis fits the intended single-cost reading?
options: And joins repairs and inspections within the complement of singular cost.
And joins cost and inspections as two main subjects, so has must be plural.
Has agrees with inspections because inspection work is conceptually one service.
Repairs and inspections form a plural subject, while cost is its object.
items.answer: And joins repairs and inspections within the complement of singular cost.
items.explanation: The cost covers two kinds of work, but one singular cost is what has risen.

rationales.And joins cost and inspections as two ma: The stated single figure covers both services; inspections is coordinated with repairs inside the of phrase.
rationales.Has agrees with inspections because insp: Has agrees with the head cost, not with inspections treated as an abstract activity.
rationales.Repairs and inspections form a plural su: The clause has no such object relation; cost heads the subject noun phrase.
rationales.And joins repairs and inspections within: The cost covers two kinds of work, but one singular cost is what has risen.

findings: The appendix findings sentence used basic singular-verb foils beneath a repetitive recommendation tail.
audit.microSkill: Coordination embedded inside a singular subject's complement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes and within an of phrase from and joining main subjects.
audit.levelReason: Determining the level of coordination is an advanced phrase-structure decision.
audit.similarityNote: Nested coordination, not merely a singular noun before a simple plural of complement.

items.setupText: Both the editor and the reviewers were concerned. A revision should give the editor a full clause and use an as-clause for the reviewers.
items.taskText: Which sentence preserves that meaning and standard agreement?
options: The editor was concerned, as was the reviewers.
The editor was concerned, as were the reviewers.
The editor was concerned, as the reviewers were not.
The editor was not concerned, as were the reviewers.
items.answer: The editor was concerned, as were the reviewers.
items.explanation: The first clause agrees with editor; the inverted as-clause has plural reviewers as its subject and repeats were concerned elliptically.

rationales.The editor was concerned, as were the re: The first clause agrees with editor; the inverted as-clause has plural reviewers as its subject and repeats were concerned elliptically.
rationales.The editor was concerned, as was the rev: The postverbal subject reviewers is plural, so the as-clause needs were.
rationales.The editor was concerned, as the reviewe: This denies concern among the reviewers, changing the stated shared reaction.
rationales.The editor was not concerned, as were th: This denies the editor's concern and no longer expresses the required shared positive state.

findings: The not-only mixed-number sentence combined a disputed usage choice with crude fragments and a tense-clashing tail.
audit.microSkill: Independent agreement in an elliptical inverted as-clause
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recasts mixed subjects as separate clauses without letting the first subject control the second auxiliary.
audit.levelReason: A constrained edit requires both clause-level agreement and preservation of a shared state.
audit.similarityNote: Agreement inside a comparative-style as-clause, not licensing inversion or testing emphatic scope.

items.setupText: A deliberately formal declaration reads, 'It is I who am responsible for the inventory.'
items.taskText: Which comment explains the agreement without declaring everyday alternatives invalid?
options: The focused I supports am in this formal pattern; me with who's is an everyday alternative.
Who is grammatically third person here, so am should be changed to is.
The form am establishes a contrast with an unnamed second-person addressee.
Am attaches the relative clause to the opening it rather than to the focused pronoun.
items.answer: The focused I supports am in this formal pattern; me with who's is an everyday alternative.
items.explanation: The formal I/who am pattern and the ordinary It's me who's responsible pattern are both established. Their different case and agreement choices belong to different constructions and registers.

rationales.Who is grammatically third person here,: In this deliberately formal construction, who can take first-person agreement from the focused I. The proposed correction overlooks that pattern.
rationales.The focused I supports am in this formal: The formal I/who am pattern and the ordinary It's me who's responsible pattern are both established. Their different case and agreement choices belong to different constructions and registers.
rationales.The form am establishes a contrast with: Am follows first-person I here, but the grammar does not establish that the intended contrast is specifically with you.
rationales.Am attaches the relative clause to the o: The opening it controls is in the cleft frame. The focused I, not it, supports am in the relative clause.

findings: The neither-charts-nor-chart sentence repeated the same unclear coordination and generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Person agreement in a formal personal-pronoun cleft
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates formal I/who am from ordinary me/who's without condemning either register.
audit.levelReason: Person, case, register, and clause structure interact in one accepted formal sentence.
audit.similarityNote: First-person relative agreement, not an elementary I am rule.

items.setupText: An editor compares 'The main problem is the travel expenses' with 'The travel expenses are the main problem.'
items.taskText: Why need the two versions not use the same form of be?
options: Each version agrees with its own subject: singular problem or plural expenses.
The version with is describes one expense, while the version with are describes several.
Be agrees with whichever noun phrase supplies the identifying information after it.
The singular version requires an understood one of before the travel expenses.
items.answer: Each version agrees with its own subject: singular problem or plural expenses.
items.explanation: Reversing the identifying sentence changes which noun phrase occupies the subject position and thus the ordinary agreement.

rationales.The version with is describes one expens: Both sentences refer to the travel expenses as plural; singular agreement in the first does not reduce the expenses to one.
rationales.Be agrees with whichever noun phrase sup: The noun phrase after be is the complement. These examples show ordinary agreement with the preceding subject, not a rule based on which phrase supplies new information.
rationales.Each version agrees with its own subject: Reversing the identifying sentence changes which noun phrase occupies the subject position and thus the ordinary agreement.
rationales.The singular version requires an underst: The first version can identify the expenses collectively as the problem. No omitted one of is needed to select one expense.

findings: The series-of-errors item repeated a basic head-noun choice with an evaluation-form tail.
audit.microSkill: Agreement after reversing an identifying copular sentence
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates grammatical subject number from the number of entities named in the complement.
audit.levelReason: Two equivalent identifications have different subject structures and agreement.
audit.similarityNote: Ordinary reversible noun-phrase identification, contrasting with variable what-clefts.

items.setupText: A cashier says, 'Five dollars is enough for the fare.' Later, describing five separate one-dollar coins, she says, 'Five dollars were scattered across the counter.'
items.taskText: Which explanation fits the different agreement choices?
options: Present tense requires singular money agreement, while past tense requires plural.
Enough makes any preceding subject singular, regardless of what it names.
The second sentence must describe a larger total because its verb is plural.
The first describes a total sum; the second describes individual monetary units.
items.answer: The first describes a total sum; the second describes individual monetary units.
items.explanation: A monetary total can take singular agreement, while separately considered coins or monetary units can take plural agreement.

rationales.Present tense requires singular money ag: Tense does not impose that distinction; the difference is amount versus separate units.
rationales.Enough makes any preceding subject singu: Enough does not mechanically control agreement; the sum is being construed as one amount.
rationales.The second sentence must describe a larg: Both totals are five dollars; plural agreement need not imply a higher monetary value.
rationales.The first describes a total sum; the sec: A monetary total can take singular agreement, while separately considered coins or monetary units can take plural agreement.

findings: The what-matters accuracy sentence merely changed forms to messages and reused basic foils.
audit.microSkill: Money as a single sum versus separate units
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains agreement variation through the intended referent rather than tense or value.
audit.levelReason: An identical measure phrase changes construal across two natural uses.
audit.similarityNote: Two readings of a measure, extending A2's explicitly single duration.

items.setupText: A financial note refers to the same money first as the proceeds of a sale and later as the income from that sale.
items.taskText: Which standard written agreement contrast is appropriate?
options: The proceeds has been transferred; the income has been recorded.
The proceeds have been transferred; the income has been recorded.
The proceeds have been transferred; the income have been recorded.
The proceeds has been transferred; the income have been recorded.
items.answer: The proceeds have been transferred; the income has been recorded.
items.explanation: Proceeds is conventionally plural in this financial meaning, whereas income is an uncountable singular noun, even when they refer to the same money.

rationales.The proceeds have been transferred; the: Proceeds is conventionally plural in this financial meaning, whereas income is an uncountable singular noun, even when they refer to the same money.
rationales.The proceeds has been transferred; the i: The shared amount does not remove the lexical plural agreement of proceeds.
rationales.The proceeds have been transferred; the: Income is uncountable singular in this meaning and requires has.
rationales.The proceeds has been transferred; the i: This reverses the established number of both nouns: proceeds plural, income singular.

findings: The findings-in-appendix item repeated the same basic form errors and a publication tail.
audit.microSkill: Different grammatical number for nouns with the same financial referent
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows why real-world identity of the money does not force identical noun agreement.
audit.levelReason: The decision depends on lexical number rather than the amount or number of transfers.
audit.similarityNote: Same referent with different noun classes, not a repeated count-versus-mass percentage.

items.setupText: In conversation, an organiser says, 'There's a lectern and two chairs on the stage.'
items.taskText: Which editing comment respects the spoken construction while offering straightforward formal agreement?
options: The singular indicates that the speaker considers the chairs part of the lectern itself.
The spoken wording is singular because two chairs is the object of there's.
The spoken singular is possible; a subject-first recast gives plural agreement.
The recast would need singular is because the first noun phrase remains a lectern.
items.answer: The spoken singular is possible; a subject-first recast gives plural agreement.
items.explanation: A clear formal recast is 'A lectern and two chairs are on the stage.' The original conversational list can begin with singular agreement when its first item is singular.

rationales.The singular indicates that the speaker: Singular agreement at the start of this existential list does not collapse the distinct objects into parts of one lectern.
rationales.The spoken singular is possible; a subje: A clear formal recast is 'A lectern and two chairs are on the stage.' The original conversational list can begin with singular agreement when its first item is singular.
rationales.The spoken wording is singular because t: Existential be does not take two chairs as an object. The two chairs are additional items introduced by the existential list.
rationales.The recast would need singular is becaus: Once the whole list is the ordinary preceding subject, its three separate objects support plural are; the first item's number is not enough.

findings: The not-only reviewers/editor sentence repeated a mixed-number prescription with crude auxiliary errors.
audit.microSkill: Existential list agreement versus a subject-first formal recast
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes an accepted conversational pattern from a clear editorial restructuring.
audit.levelReason: The location of a mixed-number coordinated subject affects the usage judgment.
audit.similarityNote: Mixed existential listing, not A2's simple there's plus an immediately plural noun.

items.setupText: One person holds both offices. The minutes say, 'Our secretary and treasurer has submitted her report.'
items.taskText: Which account of has fits this stipulated role arrangement?
options: Has agrees with report because the document, not its author, is singular.
And forces plural agreement even when both titles identify the same person.
The coordinated titles identify a single office-holder, so singular agreement is appropriate.
Has implies that only the treasurer submitted a report and the secretary did not.
items.answer: The coordinated titles identify a single office-holder, so singular agreement is appropriate.
items.explanation: Secretary and treasurer names two roles of the same person in this context, not two independent subjects.

rationales.Has agrees with report because the docum: Report is the object; the subject's single-person reference explains has.
rationales.And forces plural agreement even when bo: Titles can jointly name one individual; such co-reference supports singular agreement.
rationales.The coordinated titles identify a single: Secretary and treasurer names two roles of the same person in this context, not two independent subjects.
rationales.Has implies that only the treasurer subm: Both roles belong to the same person; singular agreement does not exclude one role-holder.

findings: Neither the lesson plans nor the lesson plan repeated the same unclear mixed-number set.
audit.microSkill: Coordinated role nouns with one referent
audit.pedagogicalValue: Makes reference, not the mere presence of and, determine singular versus plural agreement.
audit.levelReason: Two coordinated titles must be understood as co-referring under the stated context.
audit.similarityNote: One person with two roles, rather than a unified process made of two activities.

items.setupText: A news draft says, 'An estimated five hundred residents have received the notice.'
items.taskText: Which explanation correctly accounts for plural have despite an?
options: The phrase names one estimated total, so has is required even though residents is plural.
An should be removed because plural agreement rules out this estimated-number construction.
Estimated is a past-tense verb here, so the following have should be changed to had.
An belongs to the estimated-number expression; the residents remain a plural subject.
items.answer: An belongs to the estimated-number expression; the residents remain a plural subject.
items.explanation: An estimated plus a numeral is an established quantity expression; the people counted still form a plural subject.

rationales.The phrase names one estimated total, so: The sentence says that the residents received notices, not that an abstract estimated total received one. The quantity expression supports plural have.
rationales.An should be removed because plural agre: An estimated followed by a numeral is an established construction. The article can remain while the quantified residents take plural agreement.
rationales.Estimated is a past-tense verb here, so: Estimated modifies the number; it is not the sentence's finite past-tense verb. Have received supplies the finite present-perfect predicate.
rationales.An belongs to the estimated-number expre: An estimated plus a numeral is an established quantity expression; the people counted still form a plural subject.

findings: The series-of-errors sentence was repeated under a risk-assessment tail with basic form giveaways.
audit.microSkill: A singular article inside an estimated-number expression with a plural subject
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids letting the first determiner override the plural count it introduces.
audit.levelReason: The construction superficially mixes a singular article with a plural quantified noun phrase.
audit.similarityNote: Article within a quantity expression, not a number-invariant lexical head such as series.

items.setupText: A researcher writes, 'The estimates have changed again, which is inconvenient for the planning team.'
items.taskText: Why does is not have to become are to match estimates?
options: Which takes singular agreement because its spelling does not contain a plural ending.
Which singles out one particular estimate from the set as the inconvenient one.
Is agrees with the singular planning team at the end of the sentence.
Which refers to the whole change just reported, not to the estimates as plural objects.
items.answer: Which refers to the whole change just reported, not to the estimates as plural objects.
items.explanation: A sentential relative can refer back to a complete event or proposition; that singular reference supports which is inconvenient.

rationales.Which refers to the whole change just re: A sentential relative can refer back to a complete event or proposition; that singular reference supports which is inconvenient.
rationales.Which takes singular agreement because i: The form which does not display number, but it can represent singular or plural antecedents. Its reference, not its spelling, matters.
rationales.Which singles out one particular estimat: The sentence comments on the estimates' changing again. It does not select one estimate as a singular antecedent.
rationales.Is agrees with the singular planning tea: Planning team is inside the for-phrase. It identifies who is inconvenienced, not the subject controlling is.

findings: The what-matters accuracy item repeated the same skeleton with manuals substituted.
audit.microSkill: A sentential relative referring to an event or proposition
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes whole-clause which from a relative pronoun representing a nearby plural noun.
audit.levelReason: The agreement decision depends on identifying a non-noun antecedent.
audit.similarityNote: Whole-clause reference, beyond relative clauses attached to people or reports.

items.setupText: A review treats two separate facts as independent reasons for delay: the files were missing, and the backup failed.
items.taskText: Which sentence reflects that two-fact structure with standard agreement?
options: That the files were missing and that the backup failed is two distinct reasons for the delay.
That the files were missing and that the backup failed is one combined reason for the delay.
That the files were missing is the only reason for the delay.
That the files were missing and that the backup failed are two distinct reasons for the delay.
items.answer: That the files were missing and that the backup failed are two distinct reasons for the delay.
items.explanation: Each that clause contributes one fact; coordinating them as two distinct reasons supports plural agreement.

rationales.That the files were missing and that the: The explicitly separate that clauses are presented as two reasons, so the coordinated subject takes are.
Each that clause contributes one fact; coordinating them as two distinct reasons supports plural agreement.
This can express a unified construal, but the task explicitly preserves two independent reasons.
rationales.That the files were missing is the only: This drops the independently relevant backup failure and changes the number of reasons.

findings: The findings-in-appendix item again used elementary subject endings under a vote tail.
audit.microSkill: Coordinated content clauses construed as two separate facts
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a plural coordination of clauses from one clausal subject or one unified fact.
audit.levelReason: The writing goal specifies the conceptual grouping of two full subject clauses.
audit.similarityNote: Two independent propositions, rather than two activities treated as one process.

items.setupText: An editor asks, 'Which of these files are missing?' The assistant replies, 'Only the January file.'
items.taskText: Which judgment of this exchange is most accurate?
options: The answer is inconsistent because are proves at least two files must be missing.
The question has to use is because which is inherently singular.
The question allows several files as an answer without ruling out just one.
The reply is an unfinished correction of the question rather than an answer to it.
items.answer: The question allows several files as an answer without ruling out just one.
items.explanation: Plural agreement opens a potentially plural selection; the response can narrow the result to one file.

rationales.The answer is inconsistent because are p: The question can anticipate several possibilities without asserting how many files will satisfy the description.
rationales.The question has to use is because which: Which can introduce singular or plural selection; it has no fixed singular number.
rationales.The question allows several files as an: Plural agreement opens a potentially plural selection; the response can narrow the result to one file.
rationales.The reply is an unfinished correction of: Only the January file is a sufficient short answer identifying the missing member. It need not be treated as a correction simply because it supplies one file.

findings: The not-only reviewers/editor item was repeated under an appendix tail and treated proximity as a bare universal.
audit.microSkill: Plural selection in a question without a guaranteed plural answer
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates the grammar of an open selection question from a factual count established by its answer.
audit.levelReason: The learner must avoid turning interrogative number into an asserted result.
audit.similarityNote: Number in an information question, not a declarative quantifier or fixed group count.

items.setupText: After inspecting an empty building, an officer says, 'All is quiet.' After checking the waiting guests, a host says, 'All are ready.'
items.taskText: Which explanation accounts for the change in number?
options: Quiet requires a singular subject, whereas ready requires a plural subject.
All is an omitted form of all the guests in both statements.
All refers first to the overall situation, then to the waiting people.
Are means every guest is ready at a different time rather than together.
items.answer: All refers first to the overall situation, then to the waiting people.
items.explanation: Standalone all can mean everything in a situation or all the people or things in a set; that reference controls singular or plural agreement.

rationales.Quiet requires a singular subject, where: Both adjectives can describe singular or plural subjects. The different referents of all explain the number choices.
rationales.All is an omitted form of all the guests: The first statement follows an inspection of an empty building and summarizes its overall condition, not the readiness of guests.
rationales.Are means every guest is ready at a diff: Plural agreement identifies multiple people without specifying different readiness times.
rationales.All refers first to the overall situatio: Standalone all can mean everything in a situation or all the people or things in a set; that reference controls singular or plural agreement.

findings: The neither-agendas-nor-agenda sentence was another repeated and poorly distinguished coordination.
audit.microSkill: Standalone all with situation versus plural-person reference
audit.pedagogicalValue: Interprets number from all's referent rather than assigning all one fixed agreement pattern.
audit.levelReason: An implicit reference shift must be recovered from two short situations.
audit.similarityNote: All without an explicit noun complement, unlike B1 all of the equipment.

items.setupText: A proposal says, 'If this room were larger, we could hold the rehearsal here.' A proofreader flags were because room is singular.
items.taskText: Which response correctly distinguishes mood from ordinary number agreement?
options: Were indicates that this room is being treated as several connected rooms.
Were can mark an unreal condition with a singular subject, so this is not a plural-agreement error.
Were needs to become was because an unreal condition still requires ordinary singular agreement.
Were reports a past fact, so the proposal implies that the room used to be larger.
items.answer: Were can mark an unreal condition with a singular subject, so this is not a plural-agreement error.
items.explanation: Irrealis were, a form used for hypothetical or unreal situations, is licensed with singular subjects in this conditional pattern.

rationales.Were can mark an unreal condition with a: Irrealis were, a form used for hypothetical or unreal situations, is licensed with singular subjects in this conditional pattern.
rationales.Were indicates that this room is being t: This room remains singular. Were marks the hypothetical construction rather than a plural reinterpretation of room.
rationales.Were needs to become was because an unre: That rule would exclude the established irrealis form. Was also occurs in some usage, but singular room does not make were an error.
rationales.Were reports a past fact, so the proposa: The if-clause considers an unreal possibility. The form does not establish a past period when the room actually was larger.

findings: The series-of-errors sentence was reused with a protocol tail and no C1 agreement-boundary decision.
audit.microSkill: Irrealis were as a boundary of ordinary singular/plural agreement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents a proofreader from treating a valid hypothetical form as accidental plural concord.
audit.levelReason: The judgment requires distinguishing grammatical mood from number in a complete conditional.
audit.similarityNote: The agreement audit of singular were, not the Modals topic's choice of a counterfactual outcome.

items.setupText: A careful report states, 'There appear to be several discrepancies in the ledger.' A reviewer proposes appears solely because the sentence begins with there.
items.taskText: Which response best addresses that reasoning?
options: Appear can agree with the later discrepancies; there does not denote one object.
Appear should be singular because to be prevents discrepancies from affecting the finite verb.
Appear is an infinitive after there, so its form is not affected by number.
Discrepancies is the object of appear, so it cannot help explain the verb's number.
items.answer: Appear can agree with the later discrepancies; there does not denote one object.
items.explanation: In this existential raising construction, the later plural noun phrase supports plural agreement on appear; there does not refer to a single object.

rationales.Appear should be singular because to be: The intervening infinitive does not block plural agreement in this construction. The later noun phrase can support appear.
rationales.Appear can agree with the later discrepa: In this existential raising construction, the later plural noun phrase supports plural agreement on appear; there does not refer to a single object.
rationales.Appear is an infinitive after there, so: Appear is the finite verb here, and to be is the infinitive. Compare the singular 'There appears to be a discrepancy.'
rationales.Discrepancies is the object of appear, s: Appear does not take discrepancies as a direct object. The existential construction links agreement to the postponed noun phrase.

findings: The what-matters accuracy item repeated the same basic skeleton under an evidence-table tail.
audit.microSkill: Agreement in existential there plus appear to be
audit.pedagogicalValue: Tracks a postponed plural noun phrase across an intervening infinitive without treating there as an ordinary singular pronoun.
audit.levelReason: The agreement controller is separated from the finite verb by a raising structure.
audit.similarityNote: Existential raising across an infinitive, beyond direct there are or locative inversion.

items.setupText: A review says, 'It is surprising that the operating costs have fallen.'
items.taskText: Which account correctly assigns the two agreement controllers?
options: Operating costs controls both verbs because the that-clause carries the main information.
It controls is in the main clause, while operating costs controls have in the that-clause.
The whole that-clause makes both finite verbs singular.
It refers to one operating cost considered separately from the remaining costs.
items.answer: It controls is in the main clause, while operating costs controls have in the that-clause.
items.explanation: Introductory it takes singular agreement outside the content clause; the embedded plural subject has its own agreement.

rationales.Operating costs controls both verbs beca: The informational importance of the costs does not merge the two clauses' grammatical subjects. Introductory it still supports is.
rationales.The whole that-clause makes both finite: The postponed clause supplies the surprising fact, but costs remains the plural subject inside that clause and takes have.
rationales.It controls is in the main clause, while: Introductory it takes singular agreement outside the content clause; the embedded plural subject has its own agreement.
rationales.It refers to one operating cost consider: It is introductory here, not a reference to one selected cost. The entire fact that the costs have fallen is what is surprising.

findings: The findings-in-appendix sentence was repeated a fourth time with basic form foils and an incomplete policy-draft tail.
audit.microSkill: Separate agreement under extraposition with introductory it
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a grammatical placeholder subject from the plural subject inside the postponed information clause.
audit.levelReason: Two agreement domains must be identified despite the informational prominence of the embedded clause.
audit.similarityNote: Extraposition rather than what-cleft specification or a quoted sentence.

items.setupText: A correction reads, 'It is the conservators who are responsible for moving the exhibits, not the guides.'
items.taskText: Why can singular is and plural are both be correct?
options: The opening it-cleft stays singular, while who represents the plural conservators.
Is agrees with the singular job of moving exhibits, while are agrees with the guides.
Is should become are because conservators follows it immediately.
Are should become is because who repeats the opening it.
items.answer: The opening it-cleft stays singular, while who represents the plural conservators.
items.explanation: The two clauses have distinct agreement patterns: it is introduces the focus, and the relative clause agrees with the plural people identified.

rationales.Is agrees with the singular job of movin: The first verb belongs to the cleft frame, and the relative who represents conservators, not the rejected guides.
rationales.Is should become are because conservator: A plural focus does not normally make the introductory it + be frame plural.
rationales.Are should become is because who repeats: Who represents the focused conservators, not the introductory it.
rationales.The opening it-cleft stays singular, whi: The two clauses have distinct agreement patterns: it is introduces the focus, and the relative clause agrees with the plural people identified.

findings: The final not-only mixed-number sentence repeated its basic alternatives under an assessment-rubric tail.
audit.microSkill: Singular it-cleft frame with a plural focused relative subject
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents nearby plural focus from changing the first verb or singular it from changing the relative verb.
audit.levelReason: The learner must distinguish the two clauses of a focus construction, not merely recognize plural nouns.
audit.similarityNote: Plural focus with singular cleft frame, complementing the formal first-person case in 3566.

items.setupText: Compare two instructions: 'Whatever remains is to be archived' and 'Whatever documents remain are to be archived.'
items.taskText: Which analysis accounts for both agreement patterns?
options: The second subject contains plural documents; the first has no such plural head.
Documents is the object of remain, so its number affects only the later passive.
The first instruction refers to one document, whereas the second refers to several.
The presence of to be archived licenses either agreement pattern in both instructions.
items.answer: The second subject contains plural documents; the first has no such plural head.
items.explanation: Whatever remains means roughly 'anything that remains' and has singular agreement. In whatever documents remain, documents supplies plural number, also reflected in are.

rationales.Documents is the object of remain, so it: Remain has no object here. Documents supplies the plural subject within the relative construction and supports both remain and are.
rationales.The first instruction refers to one docu: Singular agreement with whatever remains does not count the remaining material. It could include numerous documents.
rationales.The second subject contains plural docum: Whatever remains means roughly 'anything that remains' and has singular agreement. In whatever documents remain, documents supplies plural number, also reflected in are.
rationales.The presence of to be archived licenses: The infinitival passive does not determine the subject's number. The difference lies in the structure of the two subjects.

findings: The accuracy-of-reports frame repeated earlier bands; a nonfinite fragment and elementary endings supplied the only discrimination.
Feedback merely repeated the keyed sentence or alleged a mismatch.
audit.microSkill: Agreement in a fused relative versus a whatever phrase with an overt plural noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates grammatical number from how many documents a general instruction may cover.
audit.levelReason: Requires analysis of two superficially similar relative constructions and rejection of a misleading numerical inference.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike the C1 what-cleft item, this contrasts two subject structures rather than variable agreement with a following complement.

items.setupText: An editor encounters: 'The cost of the repairs, the insurers estimate, exceeds the original budget.' A colleague proposes exceed because insurers is plural.
items.taskText: Which response correctly analyses the proposed change?
options: The change is needed because insurers becomes the subject when inserted before exceeds.
Insurers belongs to the inserted reporting clause; cost controls exceeds.
The change is optional because either repairs or cost can head the main subject here.
Exceeds should remain, but estimate needs to become estimates to match cost.
items.answer: Insurers belongs to the inserted reporting clause; cost controls exceeds.
items.explanation: Removing the parenthetical gives 'The cost of the repairs exceeds the original budget.' The insurers estimate that proposition; their plural number controls estimate, not exceeds.

rationales.The change is needed because insurers be: Position alone does not make insurers the subject of exceeds. The inserted clause attributes an estimate to the insurers.
rationales.Insurers belongs to the inserted reporti: Removing the parenthetical gives 'The cost of the repairs exceeds the original budget.' The insurers estimate that proposition; their plural number controls estimate, not exceeds.
rationales.The change is optional because either re: The sentence concerns the cost exceeding a budget, not the repairs doing so. Repairs is inside the of-phrase and is not an alternative head on this reading.
rationales.Exceeds should remain, but estimate need: Estimate belongs to its own clause with the plural subject the insurers. The two clauses have separate agreement controllers.

findings: The validity-of-conclusions item reused a basic singular-head exercise with an unrelated hearing tail.
Its are depend and depending foils reduced C2 to elementary verb-form recognition.
audit.microSkill: Separating parenthetical reporting-clause agreement from main-clause agreement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows why an intervening finite clause cannot simply supply the nearest noun as the main verb's subject.
audit.levelReason: The learner must recover interleaved clause boundaries and evaluate an editor's plausible but incorrect repair.
audit.similarityNote: The interruption is a complete reporting clause, not another noun inside a long subject or an as-well-as phrase.

items.setupText: An editor reviews 'One in ten applicants have worked abroad.' A colleague proposes has. Neither has checked the publication's house style.
items.taskText: Which editorial advice is accurate?
options: Use has: one is singular, so the plural applicants cannot support have in an established one-in-ten construction.
Has follows the usual formal convention; have also occurs naturally, particularly in informal speech and writing.
Keep have: in ten applicants makes applicants the grammatical head of the entire subject, so has is an agreement error.
Choose by national variety: British English permits have here, whereas American English requires has even in conversational use.
items.answer: Has follows the usual formal convention; have also occurs naturally, particularly in informal speech and writing.
items.explanation: Formal prose commonly follows singular one, while informal usage often allows plural agreement with the population being discussed. Check the intended register and any house rule before presenting either choice as a required correction.

rationales.Use has: one is singular, so the plural: This extends a formal singular preference into an unrestricted prohibition. Plural agreement is established in informal one-in-N expressions with people.
rationales.Keep have: in ten applicants makes appli: The in-phrase does not simply replace one with applicants as the subject's head. Singular has follows a conventional formal pattern and is not an error.
rationales.Choose by national variety: British Engl: The variation is not a categorical British-versus-American division. Informal plural agreement is recognized in American usage guidance too; register and house convention matter.
rationales.Has follows the usual formal convention;: Formal prose commonly follows singular one, while informal usage often allows plural agreement with the population being discussed. Check the intended register and any house rule before presenting either choice as a required correction.

findings: The original absence-and-delay sentence repeated a lower-demand coordination frame with malformed verb foils.

Integration review found that the first replacement named the register contrast in advance and used implausible numerical and employment inferences; it has been replaced with competing structural and usage judgments.
audit.microSkill: Distinguishing formal one-in-N agreement from broader notional usage and false dialect prohibitions
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches editors to distinguish a formal convention from an absolute grammatical rule, without treating the nearest plural noun as a universal controller.
audit.levelReason: The neutral editorial dispute requires evaluation of three plausible but overextended grammatical or usage rules, not recognition of a stated answer or basic form error.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike ordinary percent-of clozes, the same proportion permits competing agreement conventions; the task evaluates the limits of editorial correction.

items.setupText: A draft contains 'A range of objections have been raised' and 'The range of objections is unusually broad.' No house rule specifies singular agreement after a range of.
items.taskText: Which editorial comment best accounts for this contrast?
options: Have is defensible only if range is being used as an abbreviation for several ranges.
The first use is quantifying; the second describes the breadth of the range itself.
Is must become are because the earlier sentence has already established plural agreement.
Have makes objections the speakers who raised the issue, rather than the issues raised.
items.answer: The first use is quantifying; the second describes the breadth of the range itself.
items.explanation: A range of can function as a quantity expression and occur with plural agreement; singular agreement is also used. In the second sentence, broad describes the range itself, supporting is.

rationales.The first use is quantifying; the second: A range of can function as a quantity expression and occur with plural agreement; singular agreement is also used. In the second sentence, broad describes the range itself, supporting is.
rationales.Have is defensible only if range is bein: Plural agreement with a range of objections does not require an omitted plural word. It can reflect the quantity expression and its plural complement.
rationales.Is must become are because the earlier s: The later sentence presents the range as the thing whose breadth is described. Agreement is not fixed for every occurrence of a noun by its first use.
rationales.Have makes objections the speakers who r: Objections remain the things raised in the passive construction. Verb number does not convert them into the people doing the raising.

findings: The original wrongly rejected a range of objections have under an unrestricted grammar task.
Its remaining distractors were a malformed passive and a fragment, and the feedback gave no usage distinction.
audit.microSkill: Quantificational a range of versus reference to the range as an entity
audit.pedagogicalValue: Replaces an overgeneralized singular-head prohibition with a context-sensitive account of an established construction.
audit.levelReason: Requires distinguishing functions of a superficially identical noun phrase rather than selecting has by proximity or spelling.
audit.similarityNote: Uses the original's genuine ambiguity to test quantity-expression behaviour, distinct from lexical data usage or collective people nouns.

items.setupText: A writer wants to say that both the director and the auditors have already approved the proposal. Keep their subjects in separate coordinated clauses, use the present perfect in both, and share the final words approved the proposal.
items.taskText: Which sentence meets all three editing requirements?
options: The director and the auditors have approved the proposal.
The director had, and the auditors have, approved the proposal.
The director has approved the proposal, and so have the auditors.
The director has, and the auditors have, approved the proposal.
items.answer: The director has, and the auditors have, approved the proposal.
items.explanation: Has agrees with the director and have with the auditors. The clauses share approved the proposal, while each retains its own present-perfect auxiliary.

rationales.The director and the auditors have appro: This is grammatical and preserves the approval claim, but combines the subjects into one clause instead of retaining separate clauses.
rationales.The director had, and the auditors have,: Each auxiliary agrees with its subject, but had changes the director's clause to the past perfect, contrary to the requested tense in both clauses.
rationales.The director has, and the auditors have,: Has agrees with the director and have with the auditors. The clauses share approved the proposal, while each retains its own present-perfect auxiliary.
rationales.The director has approved the proposal,: This expresses the right facts and tense, but approved the proposal occurs in the first clause rather than as the shared final wording.

findings: The evidence-together-with-notes sentence repeated a basic parenthetical agreement check.
A have suggests foil was malformed without testing a sophisticated agreement decision.
audit.microSkill: Separate agreement-bearing auxiliaries before a shared final participial phrase
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how coordinated clauses can share wording without forcing their finite auxiliaries into the same form.
audit.levelReason: All alternatives are grammatical; the learner must satisfy simultaneous structural, tense and information-preservation constraints.
audit.similarityNote: Tests shared final material, not the C1 as-clause with an omitted predicate or the beginner and-subject rule.

items.setupText: An archivist writes, 'The donor insisted that the original manuscript be returned before the exhibition.' An editor changes be to is solely because manuscript is singular.
items.taskText: Which assessment of that change is accurate?
options: Be shows that the donor is uncertain whether the manuscript is a single object.
Is preserves the same construction because insisted automatically makes the following verb subjunctive.
Be can express the demanded action; changing it to is is not a number-agreement repair.
Be is an infinitive whose understood subject is the donor rather than the manuscript.
items.answer: Be can express the demanded action; changing it to is is not a number-agreement repair.
items.explanation: This is a mandative subjunctive: a base verb form used for an action being demanded. It can have a singular subject. Is is an indicative form, so the proposed substitution concerns the construction and reading, not a missing singular ending.

rationales.Be shows that the donor is uncertain whe: The form does not express uncertainty about the noun's number. The subject still denotes the original manuscript.
rationales.Be can express the demanded action; chan: This is a mandative subjunctive: a base verb form used for an action being demanded. It can have a singular subject. Is is an indicative form, so the proposed substitution concerns the construction and reading, not a missing singular ending.
rationales.Is preserves the same construction becau: Insisted can introduce a demand or an asserted claim. Its presence does not make the indicative form is into a subjunctive.
rationales.Be is an infinitive whose understood sub: The that-clause has its own stated subject, the original manuscript. This use of be is not a subjectless infinitive controlled by the donor.

findings: The charts variant of what matters most repeated the reports item without a new decision.
The final context tail did not raise the elementary form discrimination to C2.
audit.microSkill: Recognizing a finite mandative base form that is not defective singular agreement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents an agreement edit from overwriting the grammatical expression of a demand.
audit.levelReason: Requires distinguishing clause type, mood and reference in an editorial decision with plausible grammatical analyses.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike C1 irrealis were, this concerns the finite base form in a demand clause, with no modal-meaning inference task.

items.setupText: Consider: 'Not one of the reports that the inspectors say were altered contains the original signature.'
items.taskText: Which analysis correctly links all three finite verbs to their subjects?
options: Say follows inspectors, were refers back to reports, and contains follows not one.
Say follows reports, were follows inspectors, and contains follows the original signature.
Say follows inspectors, while were and contains both follow reports within the relative clause.
Say and were both follow inspectors, while contains agrees with the whole negative relative clause.
items.answer: Say follows inspectors, were refers back to reports, and contains follows not one.
items.explanation: The relative construction spans the intervening reporting words the inspectors say: the reports were altered. The main subject remains not one, giving contains, while inspectors controls say.

rationales.Say follows reports, were follows inspec: The inspectors do the saying, the reports were altered, and not one is the main subject. Signature is the object of contains.
rationales.Say follows inspectors, while were and c: Were belongs to the relative construction about the reports. Contains is outside that construction and makes the main claim about not one.
rationales.Say and were both follow inspectors, whi: The inspectors are not said to have been altered. The main subject is the noun phrase not one of the reports, not the relative clause that modifies reports.
rationales.Say follows inspectors, were refers back: The relative construction spans the intervening reporting words the inspectors say: the reports were altered. The main subject remains not one, giving contains, while inspectors controls say.

findings: The conclusions-in-an-interpretive-framework version was only a new tail on the same singular-head sentence.
Its rationale misclassified a fragment with depending as merely a number mismatch.
audit.microSkill: Tracking agreement across an embedded reporting clause inside a relative modifier
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches the learner to recover the relative subject across intervening words while keeping the main negative subject separate.
audit.levelReason: Three interleaved finite relationships and a long-distance relative dependency must be resolved, not just the last noun before a verb.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike the inserted insurers estimate item, the reporting clause is integrated inside a relative construction and the main subject is quantificational.

items.setupText: A British report says, 'The committee disagree among themselves about the timetable.' A publisher asks for wording that avoids collective-noun agreement variation while preserving the disagreement described.
items.taskText: Which rewrite best meets the publisher's request?
options: The committee disagrees with its members about the timetable.
The committees disagree with one another about the timetable.
The committee members disagree with one another about the timetable.
The committee's disagreement with the timetable remains unresolved.
items.answer: The committee members disagree with one another about the timetable.
items.explanation: Members supplies an explicitly plural subject, and with one another preserves disagreement within the committee. The original plural collective agreement is possible in British English, not an error that must be corrected everywhere.

rationales.The committee members disagree with one: Members supplies an explicitly plural subject, and with one another preserves disagreement within the committee. The original plural collective agreement is possible in British English, not an error that must be corrected everywhere.
rationales.The committee disagrees with its members: This contrasts the committee as a body with its own members. The original describes disagreement among the members themselves.
rationales.The committees disagree with one another: This makes several committees the disputing parties. The original concerns members within one committee.
rationales.The committee's disagreement with the ti: This presents opposition to the timetable as the committee's position. It does not preserve the internal disagreement about it.

findings: The appellate-review neither/nor item repeated the same two singular alternatives and undiagnostic messages.
Malformed verb strings made the apparent advanced context incidental.
audit.microSkill: Recasting collective agreement while preserving reciprocal internal disagreement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that a publication-oriented rewrite must retain who disagrees with whom, not just produce a singular verb.
audit.levelReason: Four grammatical rewrites compete on reference and reciprocal meaning under a usage-neutral editing goal.
audit.similarityNote: Goes beyond B2 acceptance of group was/were by requiring a dialect-neutral recast that preserves the participants in disagreement.

items.setupText: A partnership agreement says, 'Each partner and each supplier has its own account.' A reader argues that singular has means that the partners and suppliers share one account.
items.taskText: Which response best explains the grammar and its consequence for that reading?
options: Has treats partner and supplier as two job titles held by the same person.
Repeated each distributes the statement; singular has does not imply a shared account.
Has applies the account requirement only to each supplier, the nearer subject.
The sentence needs have before own can refer separately to partners and suppliers.
items.answer: Repeated each distributes the statement; singular has does not imply a shared account.
items.explanation: Each partner and each supplier supports singular agreement in formal usage. With its own account, the sentence assigns an account individually; it does not describe one account shared by everyone.

rationales.Has treats partner and supplier as two j: Nothing in the sentence requires a person to hold both roles. Each distributes the requirement across members of both named categories.
rationales.Repeated each distributes the statement;: Each partner and each supplier supports singular agreement in formal usage. With its own account, the sentence assigns an account individually; it does not describe one account shared by everyone.
rationales.Has applies the account requirement only: The coordinated subject includes both each partner and each supplier. Agreement does not remove partners from the requirement.
rationales.The sentence needs have before own can r: The distributive each construction already permits the individual reading with has. A plural verb is not needed to create separate account holders.

findings: The technical-memorandum range item repeated an ambiguous key that excluded established plural agreement.
Neither the explanation nor its generic wrong messages identified the quantity-expression issue.
audit.microSkill: Distributive coordination with repeated each and the limits of singular-number inference
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates singular agreement in an individual-by-individual requirement from a claim of joint possession.
audit.levelReason: The task evaluates a consequential interpretation of a formal clause through grammar, rather than asking which ending follows each.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike A2 each apartment or C1 co-referential job titles, this has repeated distributive determiners across two categories.

items.setupText: A rulebook says, 'A majority is required for the motion to pass.' A meeting record says, 'A majority of the delegates are absent.'
items.taskText: Which account explains the different agreement without changing either statement's meaning?
options: The rule concerns exactly one voter, whereas the record concerns several voters.
The record implies that each absent delegate personally holds a majority of votes.
The record should use is unless the meeting has more than one distinct majority.
The rule names a required threshold; the record predicates absence of people.
items.answer: The rule names a required threshold; the record predicates absence of people.
items.explanation: In the rule, a majority is the requirement considered as one threshold. In the record, a majority of the delegates can take plural agreement because the delegates are the people described as absent.

rationales.The rule concerns exactly one voter, whe: A required majority is a threshold for support, not a single voter. The singular verb does not determine the number needed.
rationales.The record implies that each absent dele: A majority of the delegates identifies a proportion of the people. It does not give a majority of voting power to each one.
rationales.The rule names a required threshold; the: In the rule, a majority is the requirement considered as one threshold. In the record, a majority of the delegates can take plural agreement because the delegates are the people described as absent.
rationales.The record should use is unless the meet: Plural agreement with a majority of people does not require multiple majorities. It can reflect the people making up the majority.

findings: The evidence-and-interview-notes variant only changed the concluding context phrase.
Its messages recycled the same unspecified mismatch claim, including for have suggests.
audit.microSkill: Majority as a required threshold versus a quantifying expression over people
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains a meaning-sensitive agreement contrast without inferring one voter or multiple majorities from verb number.
audit.levelReason: Requires distinguishing abstract threshold reference from a quantified population in two different discourse functions.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike the range item, the singular use denotes a decision threshold rather than the breadth of a set of issues.

items.setupText: A meeting secretary asks, 'No one has withdrawn their objection, have they?' A reviewer thinks has and have cannot both belong in this question.
items.taskText: Which response correctly explains both agreement and the checking question's polarity?
options: Have shows that the secretary now assumes several people have withdrawn their objections.
The tag should use hasn't because the first clause contains no negative auxiliary.
No one takes has; the tag uses they with have and checks the negative claim.
The singular verb is appropriate only if their refers to someone outside the meeting.
items.answer: No one takes has; the tag uses they with have and checks the negative claim.
items.explanation: No one has singular agreement in the main clause. They can refer back without specifying gender and takes have in the tag. Since no one makes the statement negative, the positive tag is appropriate for checking it.

rationales.Have shows that the secretary now assume: They with have does not assert a plural group of withdrawals. The tag checks the preceding claim that no person has withdrawn an objection.
rationales.The tag should use hasn't because the fi: No one makes the first clause negative even though has is not contracted with not. The ordinary opposite-polarity checking tag is therefore positive.
rationales.No one takes has; the tag uses they with: No one has singular agreement in the main clause. They can refer back without specifying gender and takes have in the tag. Since no one makes the statement negative, the positive tag is appropriate for checking it.
rationales.The singular verb is appropriate only if: Their can refer back to the people considered individually by no one. No outside person is needed to license either their or the tag's they.

findings: The lesson-plans version of what matters most reused a singular-complement choice already repeated across levels.
Neither its unexplained generic messages nor the caveat tail supplied C2 demand.
audit.microSkill: Different local agreement in an indefinite-negative statement and its they tag
audit.pedagogicalValue: Integrates pronoun reference, local verb agreement and polarity without inferring actual withdrawals from plural-looking they.
audit.levelReason: The learner must rebut an editorial objection using three interacting grammatical properties, with no malformed-form shortcut.
audit.similarityNote: Extends beyond the B1 everyone/they sequence to a negative quantifier and an opposite-polarity checking tag.

items.setupText: A writer means that the gardeners live nearby and that their niece manages the cafe. The draft says, 'The niece of the gardeners who lives nearby manages the cafe.'
items.taskText: Which rewrite uses relative-clause agreement to express the intended relationships, without adding a claim about where the niece lives?
options: The niece of the gardeners who live nearby manages the cafe.
The niece, who lives near the gardeners, manages the cafe.
The gardeners whose niece lives nearby manage the cafe.
The niece and the gardeners, who live nearby, manage the cafe.
items.answer: The niece of the gardeners who live nearby manages the cafe.
items.explanation: Plural live links who to gardeners, while singular manages links the main claim to niece. The sentence no longer makes the relative clause describe the niece's residence.

rationales.The niece of the gardeners who live near: Plural live links who to gardeners, while singular manages links the main claim to niece. The sentence no longer makes the relative clause describe the niece's residence.
rationales.The niece, who lives near the gardeners,: This locates the niece near the gardeners. It does not say that the gardeners live nearby, and it adds a residence relation the writer did not intend.
rationales.The gardeners whose niece lives nearby m: This makes the gardeners the cafe managers and the niece the nearby resident, reversing both intended assignments.
rationales.The niece and the gardeners, who live ne: This adds the gardeners as cafe managers and can include the niece among the nearby residents. The original goal assigns cafe management only to the niece.

findings: The published-corrigendum sentence recycled the same validity-of-conclusions singular-head exercise.
Its incorrect options included both a fragment and are depend rather than competing advanced readings.
audit.microSkill: Using agreement to reattach a relative clause while preserving the main predicate's subject
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how a grammatical-looking sentence can assign the right actions to the wrong people, and how a targeted edit repairs that.
audit.levelReason: All alternatives are grammatical; the choice must preserve two independent participant relationships and avoid an added residence claim.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike the B2 one-of clozes, this is a reference-preserving rewrite across two different people-denoting noun phrases.

items.setupText: A researcher writes, 'I am a linguist who studies workplace conversations.' An editor proposes study, arguing that who ultimately refers to the first-person speaker.
items.taskText: Which assessment correctly distinguishes reference from the relative clause's grammatical antecedent?
options: Who modifies a linguist here, so studies need not agree directly with I.
Study is required because two expressions referring to one person must share grammatical person.
Studies is appropriate only if the linguist is someone other than the writer.
Am makes the whole sentence first person, but studies is retained as reported speech.
items.answer: Who modifies a linguist here, so studies need not agree directly with I.
items.explanation: The relative clause is attached to a linguist, which supports third-person singular studies. In a different construction such as 'I, who study these conversations, ...', who would attach directly to I.

rationales.Study is required because two expression: Different expressions for the same person need not have the same grammatical person. I is first person, while a linguist is a third-person noun phrase.
rationales.Who modifies a linguist here, so studies: The relative clause is attached to a linguist, which supports third-person singular studies. In a different construction such as 'I, who study these conversations, ...', who would attach directly to I.
rationales.Studies is appropriate only if the lingu: The sentence identifies the writer as a linguist. Third-person agreement inside the relative clause does not introduce a second person.
rationales.Am makes the whole sentence first person: Am does not assign first-person agreement to every later clause, and no one is being quoted or reported here. The relevant fact is the attachment to a linguist.

findings: The ethics-review neither/nor variant introduced no distinction beyond the earlier singular coordination items.
The key's generic subject-number explanation did not justify an advanced assignment.
audit.microSkill: Third-person noun-phrase antecedence despite first-person co-reference
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains why grammatical person follows the local antecedent rather than every expression's real-world referent.
audit.levelReason: Requires distinguishing grammatical attachment from identity of reference in a plausible editorial dispute.
audit.similarityNote: Contrasts with C1 it is I who am: an intervening predicate noun phrase, not I itself, anchors this relative clause.

items.setupText: Compare 'A lot of defects have appeared' with 'The cause of the defects has become clear.' A learner proposes a rule: use the number of the noun immediately after of in both constructions.
items.taskText: Which evaluation best explains why that proposed rule is unreliable?
options: The rule works in the first sentence because have is active, but fails with become because it is passive.
The rule works whenever the of-phrase begins with an indefinite article rather than the.
The rule fails because both sentences should agree with the singular word before of.
A lot of quantifies defects; cause names a separate thing about which a claim is made.
items.answer: A lot of quantifies defects; cause names a separate thing about which a claim is made.
items.explanation: In the first subject, a lot of means roughly many, and the defects are what have appeared. In the second, the cause is what has become clear. An of-phrase does not have one uniform effect on agreement.

rationales.The rule works in the first sentence bec: Has become is not passive. The difference concerns the subjects, not active versus passive voice.
rationales.The rule works whenever the of-phrase be: An article alone does not settle the structure. A cause of the defects would still name a cause and normally take singular agreement.
rationales.The rule fails because both sentences sh: That would wrongly force singular agreement in a lot of defects have appeared. A lot of functions as a quantity expression here.
rationales.A lot of quantifies defects; cause names: In the first subject, a lot of means roughly many, and the defects are what have appeared. In the second, the cause is what has become clear. An of-phrase does not have one uniform effect on agreement.

findings: The counterargument-table range sentence both repeated a template and rejected established plural agreement.
Its claim that only one sentence was complete and correct was therefore unsound.
audit.microSkill: Testing a nearest-noun agreement rule against quantifying and ordinary of-phrases
