audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents both blanket singular-head rules and blanket nearest-plural rules from replacing structural interpretation.
audit.levelReason: Requires evaluating a proposed generalization with close grammatical counteranalyses, not selecting a single familiar ending.
audit.similarityNote: Where the range item accepts variation, this comparison explains why quantity-expression behaviour cannot be generalized to cause.

items.setupText: A formal response reads, 'The redesign would save space. Be that as it may, the access problem remains.' An editor wants to replace be with is because that is singular.
items.taskText: Which comment best assesses this proposed agreement edit?
options: Be is simply the infinitive governed by the later may, with the same structure as may be.
Is is preferable because it strengthens the same concession without changing its grammatical construction.
Be is retained because the preceding would makes the following independent clause infinitival.
Be belongs to a fixed concessive expression, not an ordinary indicative statement needing is.
items.answer: Be belongs to a fixed concessive expression, not an ordinary indicative statement needing is.
items.explanation: Be that as it may is an established formal expression that sets a point aside before continuing the argument. Its be is not a missing singular indicative ending, so changing it to is does not preserve the expression.

rationales.Be belongs to a fixed concessive express: Be that as it may is an established formal expression that sets a point aside before continuing the argument. Its be is not a missing singular indicative ending, so changing it to is does not preserve the expression.
rationales.Be is simply the infinitive governed by: The opening be belongs to the concessive frame, not a reordered ordinary may be verb phrase. The expression cannot be explained by moving a modal's infinitive across its subject.
rationales.Is is preferable because it strengthens: Is that as it may does not retain the conventional concessive construction. This is not merely a stronger version of the same wording.
rationales.Be is retained because the preceding wou: Would governs save in the preceding sentence. It does not turn a separate sentence's opening expression into its infinitival complement.

findings: The final-adjudication evidence sentence was another parenthetical-number template with a specialized tail.
The have suggests foil and repeated feedback did not test advanced editorial judgment.
audit.microSkill: Recognizing formulaic concessive be as outside ordinary indicative agreement correction
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches editors not to regularize a licensed fixed construction solely from the number of its pronoun.
audit.levelReason: Requires grammatical diagnosis of a formal formula, including rejection of misleading cross-sentence and coordinated-subject analyses.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike the donor's productive demand clause, this targets a fixed concessive expression; it does not ask learners to infer a stance already named in the setup.

items.setupText: A formal narrative says, 'The last guests having left, the caretaker locks the courtyard.' A reviewer says having should become have because guests is plural.
items.taskText: Which response best diagnoses the proposed change?
options: Having left is nonfinite and has its own stated subject; it does not inflect for guests.
Having is singular because its subject is the later caretaker, while guests is its object.
Have would preserve the same nonfinite construction while making its plural agreement visible.
Having left is a shortened relative clause modifying guests, equivalent in structure to who have left.
items.answer: Having left is nonfinite and has its own stated subject; it does not inflect for guests.
items.explanation: The opening is an absolute construction: a nonfinite clause with the last guests as its subject. Having does not change for number. Replacing it with have creates a finite clause and would require different punctuation or linkage to the main clause.

rationales.Having left is nonfinite and has its own: The opening is an absolute construction: a nonfinite clause with the last guests as its subject. Having does not change for number. Replacing it with have creates a finite clause and would require different punctuation or linkage to the main clause.
rationales.Having is singular because its subject i: The guests are the people who have left; they are not an object of having. The caretaker is the separate subject of locks.
rationales.Have would preserve the same nonfinite c: Have left with the last guests as its subject is a finite present-perfect clause. It is not an inflected version of the original nonfinite construction.
rationales.Having left is a shortened relative clau: The opening supplies a background circumstance in a separate nonfinite clause. It is not a relative modifier within a noun phrase; treating it as one would leave that opening noun phrase without a role in the main clause.

findings: The agendas-in-statutory-analysis version repeated the same what-matters construction.
Its being fragment was dismissed as a number mismatch without distinguishing finiteness from agreement.
audit.microSkill: Distinguishing a subject-bearing absolute participial clause from a finite agreement domain
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows why adding an agreement-bearing verb can change clause structure and create a new punctuation problem.
audit.levelReason: Requires recognizing a formal nonfinite construction and tracing the consequences of an apparently minor editorial repair.
audit.similarityNote: The opening has its own explicit subject, unlike gerund complements or speaker-oriented judging expressions reviewed in the earlier topic.

items.setupText: An inventory report says, 'Five thousand dollars' worth of paintings have been recovered.' A colleague objects that have can be correct only if actual dollars, not paintings, were recovered.
items.taskText: Which response best addresses that objection without imposing an unstated house style?
options: Have implies that each painting was individually worth five thousand dollars.
The sentence refers to both paintings and money, with have agreeing with their combined value.
Changing have to has would mean that only one painting had been recovered.
Plural agreement can reflect paintings; it does not turn their stated value into recovered cash.
items.answer: Plural agreement can reflect paintings; it does not turn their stated value into recovered cash.
items.explanation: A monetary worth-of expression can occur with plural agreement reflecting the goods named after of. It still denotes paintings of the stated total value. A singular amount-focused version is also possible; neither reading requires recovered banknotes.

rationales.Have implies that each painting was indi: The value expression describes the quantity of paintings collectively. Plural agreement does not distribute that full value to each painting.
rationales.Plural agreement can reflect paintings;: A monetary worth-of expression can occur with plural agreement reflecting the goods named after of. It still denotes paintings of the stated total value. A singular amount-focused version is also possible; neither reading requires recovered banknotes.
rationales.The sentence refers to both paintings an: The dollars specify how much the paintings are worth. They are not an additional recovered item coordinated with paintings.
rationales.Changing have to has would mean that onl: Singular agreement can present the valued quantity as an amount. It need not reduce the number of paintings to one.

findings: The expert-testimony validity sentence was a fourth context substitution on the same C2 frame.
The foils and feedback again conflated finite agreement, malformed auxiliaries and fragments.
audit.microSkill: Agreement with a monetary worth-of expression without confusing value and physical referents
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates the grammatical presentation of an amount from the identity and number of the goods recovered.
audit.levelReason: Requires defending established agreement against several plausible but unsupported inferences about valuation and reference.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike the C1 coins item, the money names the value of other goods rather than the actual objects whose number changes.

items.setupText: Exactly one of the speaker and the addressee is to chair the session. Rewrite without making either you or I a shared subject before an agreement-sensitive verb; name both parties and keep the one-person restriction explicit.
items.taskText: Which sentence meets the editing goal?
options: You and I will decide who chairs the session, but only one chair is needed.
Either you or I am to chair the session, but not both of us.
Either you will chair the session or I will, but not both of us.
Either you and I will chair the session or neither of us will.
items.answer: Either you will chair the session or I will, but not both of us.
items.explanation: Each alternative has its own subject and will, whose form does not vary with person. The second clause omits the repeated predicate, and but not both of us preserves the explicit one-person restriction.

rationales.You and I will decide who chairs the ses: This makes the two people decision-makers. It does not require either of them to be the chair; they could choose someone else.
rationales.Either you or I am to chair the session,: This keeps the mixed-person shared subject that the editing brief asks you to avoid. The task is a structural recast, not a claim that this proximity-based form is never used.
rationales.Either you will chair the session or I w: Each alternative has its own subject and will, whose form does not vary with person. The second clause omits the repeated predicate, and but not both of us preserves the explicit one-person restriction.
rationales.Either you and I will chair the session: This offers both people together or neither person, excluding the intended exactly-one arrangement. Its agreement is grammatical but its alternatives are different.

findings: The compliance-addendum neither/nor sentence repeated the singular-absence/singular-delay item.
Its unvaried malformed distractors and generic messages supplied no new C2 distinction.
audit.microSkill: Recasting mixed-person disjunction as coordinated clauses while preserving exclusive alternatives
audit.pedagogicalValue: Provides an editing strategy for awkward person agreement without changing which participants are eligible or how many may act.
audit.levelReason: Requires coordinating syntax, ellipsis and the scope of exclusive alternatives; grammatical options fail for distinct reasons.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike C1 neither/nor unavailability, this involves mixed grammatical person, a non-inflecting modal and an explicitly exclusive future choice.

items.setupText: A report says, 'The assistant of the curator who was interviewed has resigned.' The surrounding text has mentioned interviews with both people, but does not identify which interview this sentence concerns.
items.taskText: What can an editor conclude from was about the relative clause's attachment?
options: Was proves that the curator was interviewed, because the nearest noun controls relative agreement.
Was cannot settle the attachment, since both possible antecedents are singular.
Was proves that the assistant was interviewed, because the main subject controls relative agreement.
Was cannot help because past-tense be has the same form with singular and plural subjects.
items.answer: Was cannot settle the attachment, since both possible antecedents are singular.
items.explanation: Both assistant and curator can support singular was. Agreement therefore does not disambiguate this sentence; the editor should clarify which person's interview is intended rather than treating a preferred attachment as compulsory.

rationales.Was proves that the curator was intervie: Proximity may encourage that reading, but it is not proof. The more distant assistant is also singular and can support was.
rationales.Was proves that the assistant was interv: A relative clause inside a subject phrase need not modify the phrase's head. Curator is also a possible antecedent here.
rationales.Was cannot settle the attachment, since: Both assistant and curator can support singular was. Agreement therefore does not disambiguate this sentence; the editor should clarify which person's interview is intended rather than treating a preferred attachment as compulsory.
rationales.Was cannot help because past-tense be ha: Past-tense be does distinguish singular was from plural were in ordinary statements. It cannot help here because both candidate antecedents have the same number, not because it lacks agreement.

findings: The longitudinal-model range item preserved the same false exclusion of plural have.
A model-revision tail and a generic mismatch explanation did not create a new learning point.
audit.microSkill: Recognizing when agreement cannot resolve relative-clause attachment
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches the limits of grammatical evidence and the need for clarification when competing antecedents share number.
audit.levelReason: Requires distinguishing a likely reading from a grammatically compelled one, while rejecting two plausible attachment heuristics.
audit.similarityNote: Deliberately contrasts with the niece/gardeners edit: there number distinguishes the antecedents; here it cannot.

items.setupText: A policy draft says, 'The trustees, each of whom has signed a separate declaration, are eligible to vote.' An editor proposes have in the relative clause to make both verbs plural like trustees.
items.taskText: Which response correctly evaluates the proposed change and the original declaration claim?
options: Has means one declaration was signed jointly, so have is needed to express separate declarations.
The main clause should use is because each of whom becomes the subject after the comma.
Each governs has within the relative clause; trustees governs are in the main clause.
Have is required because whom is plural, while each modifies declaration rather than the subject.
items.answer: Each governs has within the relative clause; trustees governs are in the main clause.
items.explanation: In this formal draft, each of whom has makes an individual statement about every trustee. The main subject the trustees independently takes are. Repeating one verb number across the sentence is not the agreement requirement.

rationales.Has means one declaration was signed joi: Each and a separate declaration already distribute the signing across individual trustees. Singular agreement inside that clause does not make the declaration joint.
rationales.Each governs has within the relative cla: In this formal draft, each of whom has makes an individual statement about every trustee. The main subject the trustees independently takes are. Repeating one verb number across the sentence is not the agreement requirement.
rationales.The main clause should use is because ea: The relative clause supplements the trustees; it does not replace that plural main subject. Its singular each governs only its own finite verb.
rationales.Have is required because whom is plural,: Each is the head of each of whom, not a modifier of declaration. Whom links the phrase to the trustees without making each a plural subject in the formal pattern used here.

findings: The ruling-issued evidence item was a fourth version of the same C2 parenthetical sentence.
Its correct explanation repeated the answer, and all wrong feedback asserted an unspecified mismatch.
audit.microSkill: Independent agreement and distributive reference inside an each-of-whom relative supplement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents global number matching from erasing the grammar of an embedded individual-by-individual statement.
audit.levelReason: Requires recovering nested agreement domains and distinguishing singular distributive syntax from joint versus separate document reference.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike repeated each across coordinated categories, this places each inside a supplementary relative while the main subject remains plural.
